newsitem.title: INDIA: Jiang's South Asia tour plays on old Indian fears.
newsitem.headline: Jiang's South Asia tour plays on old Indian fears.

text.p: Chinese President Jiang Zemin's visit to three South Asian neighbours could help stoke an old rivalry between China and India for political influence in the volatile region, analysts said on Wednesday.

Jiang arrived to a warm welcome in the Himalayan kingdom of Nepal on Wednesday after beginning his tour in India and then holding talks with his closest regional ally and New Delhi's arch foe, Pakistan.

India has long been worried by China's wooing of New Delhi's neighbours -- Bangladesh, Burma, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka -- with concessional arms deals that it says threaten to undercut India's ties with the regional states.

"India's biggest worry in this equation is Pakistan. China has consciously built up Pakistan as as counterweight to India," defence analyst Brahma Chellaney, of the Centre for Policy Research, told Reuters in New Delhi.
"Pakistan is the only country to which China has transferred both missile and nuclear weapons technology," he said.
Both countries deny the charge, made by the United States among others.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Gujral recently cited China's nuclear arsenal as one of the reasons for New Delhi's recent opposition to a global nuclear test ban treaty.
Gujral argued that India would be left vulnerable to a Chinese threat if it signed the treaty, open for ratification under a U.N.-backed agreement despite Delhi's opposition.

The two countries fought a brief border war in 1962 that was a humiliating defeat for India. But both agreed to improve their frozen ties in 1988 when then prime minister Rajiv Gandhi visited Beijing.

Jiang's visit to New Delhi was marked by an agreement to reduce troops and armaments along their Himalayan border. The pact fleshed out an agreement in principle signed by former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao in Beijing in 1993.
"The latest agreement is useful in that it brings to light the failures so far in implementing the 1993 accord," Chellaney wrote in Delhi's Pioneer newspaper on Wednesday.
Indian and Chinese officials say both countries, locked in major economic reforms, need an assurance of security along their sprawling borders, primarily to scale down defence spending.
Indian officials said Jiang's visit was expected to provide some comfort there.
"However, the real levers for India's political battle with China lie in extending New Delhi's ties with Southeast Asian countries, including Japan," a senior Indian diplomat told Reuters.

"We cannot ignore the fact that China's main aim is to keep India tied down to a limited role in South Asia," the official said. "Jiang's visit should not be seen for more than the fact that the two countries are talking and that they need to talk."
Jiang, in an address to the Pakistani Senate (upper house of parliament), advocated a nuclear-free zone in South Asia.
Western diplomats said the remarks targeted India's opposition to the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
"It's sort of trying to keep a little bit of pressure up on the Indians on the CTBT issue," a Beijing-based diplomat said.
Indian officials see China's annexation of Tibet, bordering India, and the crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 1959 as the start of tense ties between the two Asian giants.
Western diplomats said China's recent crackdown in Tibet could be a major factor in Jiang's first visit to South Asia.
"His trip to India, Pakistan and Nepal is not unconnected with the crackdown in Tibet -- being sure his borders are secure," said one diplomat in Beijing.
